chunks.content: Introduction Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has transformed treatment options for B-cell cancers. Genetically engineering autologous cytotoxic T cells to express a receptor recognizing cancer cell surface antigens (typically CD19 or B-cell maturation antigen, BCMA) facilitates the destruction of cancerous cells. CAR T cell therapies have improved disease outcomes for multiple myeloma, leukemia, and lymphoma. , The same T cell modifications are now being applied to treat autoreactive B-cells in autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), and multiple sclerosis (MS). , , , The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved several CAR T cell therapies for B-cell cancers. CAR T cell therapies for autoimmune disorders have received investigational new drug applications (ALLO-329, KYV-101, ATA3219, CABA071, CLBR001+SWI019) with full approvals anticipated. However, the development of new CAR T cell therapies has slowed as existing CAR T cell designs are less effective at overcoming the immunosuppressive microenvironment of solid tumors. Researchers exploring new areas of CAR T cell therapy have focused on regulatory T cells (Tregs). Tregs have been described as “the next frontier of cell-based therapy.” For their role in discovering Tregs, Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, and Shimon Sakaguchi were awarded the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While conventional CAR T cells enable the immune system to target and attack disease-causing cells, antigen-specific Tregs can treat conditions in which dysregulated immune activation damages healthy tissue and drives disease progression. CAR Treg therapies for inflammatory conditions, including graft versus host disease (GvHD), , type 1 diabetes, , inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), , asthma, and rheumatoid arthritis have been tested in animal models, with some entering clinical trials. Another area where CAR Treg therapies have the potential to be impactful is in the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. Just as diseases treated by traditional CAR T cell therapies were considered incurable, current treatments for neurodegenerative diseases offer limited abilities to halt disease progression. Previous preclinical studies have linked neurodegeneration to neuroinflammation and treated neurodegeneration with nonspecific Treg therapies. Now, multiple teams, including our own, are developing CAR Treg therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. CAR Treg therapies for neurodegenerative diseases are in their early stages and recent advances have not yet been synthesized and discussed in a review. Here, we review the state of CAR Treg therapies for neurodegenerative diseases and outline next required steps to bring these therapies to the clinic. Neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration The most common immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS) are mononuclear phagocytes (MPs), including microglia, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Like all MPs, both inside and outside the CNS, microglia are responsible for maintaining normal tissue homeostasis but can become activated in response to injury or infection. , Activated microglia are metabolically active, increase phagocytosis, and enhance cell migration and intracellular killing by releasing chemokines and biocidal factors that recruit immune cells to sites of injury or infection. Conversely, activated microglia can also mitigate damage caused by disease or immune responses by promoting tissue repair and remodeling. , , These inflammatory and protective functions are carried out by pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) microglia. In reality, microglial phenotypes are highly complex and any simple M1/M2 classification fails to fully capture their true complexity, heterogeneity, and dynamic nature. Microglial populations in different conditions exhibit a range of phenotypes, including specific disease-associated states. The complexity is compounded by the parallel participation of T effector cells (Teff) or Treg T cell subsets, requiring simplified terminology to best characterize the immune-CNS environment in disease and repair. Simplified terminology is used not only for microglia but also for astrocytes. Astrocytes can become reactive in response to exogenous and cell-specific signals , and exert neuroprotective (A2) or harmful (A1) effects. , A2 astrocytes are a type of reactive astrocyte that demonstrates neuroprotective properties by releasing beneficial neurotrophic factors, as opposed to the neurotoxic A1 cell type. Normally, the CNS also contains distinct groups of small numbers of memory T cells and Tregs, which function to manage immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis, respectively. , When immune responses within the CNS become over-activated, peripheral Tregs enter the CNS to control microglial inflammation. , Removing Tregs can exacerbate neuroinflammation and facilitate neurodegeneration. Studies have linked neurodegenerative diseases to neuroinflammatory processes and implicated the immune system in neurodegeneration. While each disease shows unique patterns of neuroinflammation, such as different cytokine profiles, other aspects are common across many neurodegenerative conditions. , Generally, the buildup of misfolded proteins—such as amyloid-β (Aβ), α-synuclein (α-syn), hyperphosphorylated tau, huntingtin, TDP-43, SOD1, or FUS—is either a product or a trigger of neuroinflammation, leading to microglial activation and the subsequent recruitment of adaptive immune cells. , For example, circulating CD4 + T cells from patients with PD release pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to α-syn, highlighting the role of T cell responses in perpetuating neuroinflammation caused by

neuroinflammatory processes and implicated the immune system in neurodegeneration. While each disease shows unique patterns of neuroinflammation, such as different cytokine profiles, other aspects are common across many neurodegenerative conditions. , Generally, the buildup of misfolded proteins—such as amyloid-β (Aβ), α-synuclein (α-syn), hyperphosphorylated tau, huntingtin, TDP-43, SOD1, or FUS—is either a product or a trigger of neuroinflammation, leading to microglial activation and the subsequent recruitment of adaptive immune cells. , For example, circulating CD4 + T cells from patients with PD release pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to α-syn, highlighting the role of T cell responses in perpetuating neuroinflammation caused by misfolded protein aggregates. In turn, increasing neuroinflammation is associated with increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and immune cell infiltration in the parenchyma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The effects of sustained, chronic neuroinflammation include synaptic loss, edema, and cell death, , and can lead to the accumulation of neurotoxic and cytotoxic metabolites. , Damage caused by immune activation leads to increased levels of cellular debris, which act as markers of “injury,” fueling further inflammation and, if unchecked, neurodegeneration. Connections between inflammation and neurodegeneration have been widely observed. The risk of developing a neurodegenerative disease correlates with an age-related increase in inflammation , and changes in the expression patterns of microglia-specific genes, making age the primary risk factor for most neurodegenerative diseases. Neurodegeneration is also linked to inflammation in other parts of the body, including the “gut-brain axis” through which intestinal inflammation can promote neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. , Imbalances in the ratio of circulating Teffs and Tregs have been linked to cognitive deficits and buildup of amyloid-β plaques in the brain. The connection between neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration has made Tregs and Treg-based platforms a major focus of new treatment strategies for neurodegenerative diseases. Regulatory T cells Tregs represent several lineages of T cells that suppress immune responses and are characterized by both their functional and immunologic recognition roles. First , Tregs serve to prevent the immune system from recognizing self-antigens and attacking the body’s own tissues, a homeostatic immune status known as immunological tolerance. Second , Tregs ensure that hyperactive immune responses to foreign antigens are suppressed and cause minimal tissue damage. Third , divergent Treg-like lineages with distinct phenotypes include CD4 + CD25hiCD127loFoxp3+ Tregs, CD8+Foxp3+ Tregs, and Tr1 cells. , , Each is more closely connected by the cell’s functional ability to inhibit immune responses than by its shared gene expression patterns. , Fourth , Tregs are generally characterized by the expression of the transcription factor forkhead box p3 (FOXP3). , Fifth , Tregs are commonly divided by their origins as thymic or natural (tTregs or nTregs) and peripheral or induced Tregs (pTregs or iTregs). Individuals born with non-functional Tregs due to genetic mutations tend to develop significant autoimmune disease at early ages. , Treg deficits and dysfunction have been linked to autoimmune and inflammatory conditions that now include expanded disease listings such as rheumatoid arthritis, , juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, asthma, and others. , These studies confirm the essential role Tregs play in limiting the potentially damaging effects of chronic or uncontrolled immune activation that underlies the pathobiology of a broad disease range. T cell populations used in conventional CAR T cell therapies include both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells that secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, IFN-γ, and TNF-α, and recognize and attack disease-causing agents. These cells are broadly known as T effector cells, or Teffs. In contrast, Tregs regulate inflammatory activity across various immune cells, including CD4 + and CD8 + Teffs, B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and DCs as well as macrophages and microglia. This suppression occurs through the release of anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10, IL-35, and transforming growth factor β (TGF-β), as well as the expression of inhibitory factors regulated by contact-dependent signaling from CTLA-4- and LAG-3-expressing Tregs. , , , Tregs limit the tissue damage caused by excessive immune responses by promoting repair and remodeling processes, such as releasing amphiregulin to promote tissue repair, , , , expressing vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to support blood vessel formation, , and directing phagocytic cells to assist in debris clearance. Tregs can also sequester essential growth factors and nutrients, depriving pro-inflammatory cells of resources, thereby inducing a state of virtual inactivity (anergy) or even programmed cell death (apoptosis) to eliminate overactive immune cells. , Tregs have been shown to promote white matter repair through the remyelination of damaged axons, , while release of amphiregulin and IL-10 prevents neuronal loss. , Tregs limit the number of pro-inflammatory astrocytes in an AD mouse model , and induce the expression of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) by astrocytes. This results in the inhibition of microglial pro-inflammatory functions during neurodegenerative diseases and following spinal cord

This results in the inhibition of microglial pro-inflammatory functions during neurodegenerative diseases and following spinal cord injury. Despite their key role in immune regulation, Tregs account for only a small fraction of peripheral blood lymphocytes. , The ratio between effector and Treg cells reflects a balance between immune activation or suppression ( ). , Chimeric antigen receptor Tregs While conventional CAR T cells enable the immune system to target and eliminate disease-causing cells, antigen-specific Tregs suppress immune responses. This function can be programmed to treat conditions in which dysregulated immune activation damages healthy tissues, leading to disease progression. CAR Tregs are being developed to treat a spectrum of inflammatory diseases, tested in relevant animal models, including graft versus host disease (GvHD), , type 1 diabetes, , inflammatory bowel disease, , asthma, hemophilia, and rheumatoid arthritis. Several clinical trials are now operational. One potential use of CAR Treg therapies lies in treating neurodegenerative diseases. Just as cancers and autoimmune diseases that previously possessed limited therapeutic options are now treated by traditional CAR T cell therapies, existing treatments for neurodegenerative diseases are also limited. Preclinical research has linked neurodegeneration to neuroinflammation, and polyclonal nonspecific Treg therapies have shown benefit. We and others are in the early stages of developing CAR Tregs for neurological disease, building on the same principles as other CAR Treg therapies. CAR Tregs exert effects opposite to those of conventional CAR T effector cells. Instead of immune activation, CAR Tregs drive tissue-cell homeostasis. This makes them more suitable for cases of immunoregulatory dysfunction. Studies of patients refractory to CAR T cell therapy for cancer have revealed that some circulating CAR T cells have acquired a CAR Treg phenotype. , These studies showed that cancer progression and lack of response to CAR T cell therapy were associated with higher levels of CAR T cells that enter Treg-like states, suggesting that the CAR Tregs suppressed conventional CAR T cells and prevented their tumoricidal activities. Depleting CAR Tregs in the initiating CAR T cell population improved tumor-killing effects. On the other hand, the pro-inflammatory actions of conventional CAR T cells can lead to complications, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and a range of neurological side effects (tremors, confusion, seizures, difficulty speaking, and other psychiatric symptoms), collectively designated as immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). , The fact that conventional CAR T cells can promote neurological symptoms characteristic of neurodegenerative diseases suggests that CAR Tregs could counter those syndromes and play a role in treating neuroinflammation-mediated neurodegenerative diseases. Recent advances in CAR Treg therapies provide further support for expanding their use in neurodegenerative diseases. Polyclonal Tregs and low-dose IL-2 have already shown promise in clinical trials for GvHD ( NCT01795573 , NCT03185000 , NCT06991361 , NCT04414111 ) and type 1 diabetes ( NCT02691247 , NCT01862120 ), although they displayed less efficacy in the latter trials. Polyclonal Tregs are isolated from a patient, expanded, and readministered without engineering. IL-2 is the cytokine that selectively stimulates Treg expansion at low doses. , Engineered Treg therapies are an attractive therapeutic option given the limited number of antigen-specific Tregs recovered during non-engineered Treg therapies. , CAR Treg therapies for GvHD have generated encouraging results in pre-clinical models of human disease , and clinical trials ( NCT04817774 , NCT05993611 ) are underway. CAR Tregs developed in preclinical models of rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disorders have also advanced to clinical testing ( NCT06361836 , NCT06201416 ). Chimeric antigen receptor Tregs alternatives Poly-specific Treg therapies using whole Treg populations have been investigated as potential treatments for inflammatory conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases. Adoptive transfer of polyclonal Tregs or in vivo expansion with low-dose IL-2 has been tested in GvHD trials ( NCT06411184 , NCT06991361 , NCT01795573 , NCT01937468 , NCT01911039 , NCT03284242 ), with results showing that treatment was well-tolerated and benefitted patients. , The same polyclonal Treg therapies have also been used in clinical trials for type 1 diabetes ( NCT01210664 , NCT06688331 , NCT02772679 ), but failed to achieve significant therapeutic effects despite showing a positive safety profile. , Regarding neurodegenerative diseases, granulocyte macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF, sargramostim), which also expands polyclonal Tregs, is being tested as a Treg stimulant in PD ( NCT01882010 ). Additionally, low-dose IL-2 is also under study as a treatment for AD ( NCT06096090 ). Despite some promise,

Additionally, low-dose IL-2 is also under study as a treatment for AD ( NCT06096090 ). Despite some promise, especially in the context of GvHD, polyclonal Treg therapies have limitations that highlight the need for antigen-specific CAR Treg therapies. Without the ability to direct Tregs to specific inflamed tissues, polyclonal Treg therapies could induce generalized immunosuppression and unintended cross-reactivity with infectious agents. This may increase vulnerability to infections, although these scenarios have not yet been observed in clinical trials. , The expansion of polyclonal Tregs and general immune suppression could elevate cancer risk, as Tregs support the tumor microenvironment and metastasis. , , Quantifying immune suppression through lymphocyte counts, cytokine profiling, and in vitro suppressive function are important parameters for determining and controlling the extent of post-therapeutic immunosuppression ( NCT05993611 ). However, no matter the extent of general immunosuppression by polyclonal Tregs, Tregs that possess antigen specificity would be significantly more potent than polyclonal Tregs because recognizing an antigen in the context of MHC is essential for activation and expansion. , , Without antigen recognition, the immunosuppressive effects of Tregs are limited to more indirect pathways or stand-by effects. In a polyclonal Treg population, it is estimated that only 8 out of 100,000 cells can afford the recognition of a dominant antigen. Thus, the use of polyclonal Tregs may partially explain the inconclusive results of early studies on the benefits of immunosuppressive therapies for neurodegeneration. , Problems related to poly-specific Treg therapies could require the development of standardized populations of antigen-specific Tregs. Engineering CAR Tregs is not the only method to generate antigen-specific Tregs. Like all T cells, each Treg expresses a specific T cell receptor (TCR) designed to recognize a specific antigen presented by the MHC on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell (APC) ( ). Due to MHC restriction, TCRs generated by one individual typically cannot recognize antigens presented by MHC molecules from another individual. This MHC restriction represents a major impediment to transplant engraftment and T cell-mediated GvHD. In the context of GvHD, graft-specific Tregs can be generated by repeatedly stimulating graft-recipient T cells with donor-derived APCs. , However, expanding antigen-specific Tregs using this method is less applicable outside of GvHD because the number of preexisting antigen-specific Tregs is likely more limited. Instead of utilizing CARs, alternate strategies design TCRs that recognize specific antigens of interest and engineer Tregs to express those TCRs. Engineered TCRs have shown promise in clinical trials but have more limited applicability than CARs since the genetic template encoding them will only work in patients who are MHC-matched. Naturally occurring TCRs that do not require MHC to bind to proteins such as amyloid-β, have been identified, but are still in the early stages of therapeutic development. , The same is true for TCRs engineered to bypass MHC restriction. Engineering chimeric antigen receptor Tregs to extend therapeutic applications CARs come in multiple iterations but typically consist of a single polypeptide chain with four basic regions ( ). The extracellular domain (1) determines antigen specificity, usually linking the heavy and light variable chains of an antibody that recognizes a specific antigen into a single-chain variable fragment (scFv). The scFv chain contains the complementary determining region 3 (CDR3), which comprises the protein’s antigen-binding region. The hinge region or spacer (2) gives the extracellular domain flexibility and space to interact with antigen epitopes, reducing steric hindrance and affecting the receptor’s properties based on hinge length. The transmembrane domain (3) anchors the CAR in the cell membrane and enables interactions with other CARs and intracellular signaling molecules. The intracellular signaling domain (4) converts antigen binding into Treg activation and typically includes an activation domain (CD3ζ) and one or more costimulatory modules (CD28, 4-1BB/CD137), which can influence Treg phenotype depending on which ones are chosen. Choosing the right CAR design is essential for developing effective CAR Treg therapies. Although CAR Tregs reflect a newer focus compared to traditional CAR T cells, studies comparing different CAR Treg designs found that a CD28 costimulatory domain maintained Tregs’ suppressive function better than 4-1BB, while another found no functional differences and deemed 4-1BB preferable for safety reasons. 4-1BB (CD137), is a costimulatory receptor expressed by activated T cells that serves to boost the immune response and was used in CAR T cell design to promote T cell proliferation, survival, and cytokine production.

CAR Tregs can also incorporate the gene encoding the Treg master transcription factor, FOXP3. In animal models of GvHD, CAR Tregs transduced with FOXP3 maintained stable FOXP3 expression and demonstrated greater therapeutic efficacy than control polyclonal Tregs and CAR Tregs lacking FOXP3. Another study testing a large panel of co-receptors found superior outcomes for those CAR Tregs constructs incorporating CD28. In preclinical studies, CD3-CD28-expressing constructs were the most common intracellular domains. Challenges to the design and manufacture of efficacious CAR Tregs include the incorporation of intracellular domains to induce and stabilize the Treg program, manage untoward toxicities, and scale to generate sufficient numbers for reproducible outcomes. Developing CAR Treg therapies also requires the ability to selectively isolate suitable Tregs from patients. As an intracellular transcription factor, FOXP3 is not a selective marker for Treg isolation. One approach involves selecting T cells with high CD4 and CD25 expression and low CD127 levels to obtain enriched CD4 + CD25hiCD127loFOXP3+ Tregs. , Another approach involves selecting recent tTreg emigrants based on CD45RA or other extracellular markers. , This method benefits from the fact that tTregs exhibit more stable epigenetic profiles than pTregs, thus supporting the retention of Treg-like properties during expansion and treatment. Another strategy to protect Treg lineage stability involves gene editing to establish permanent FOXP3 expression alongside CAR expression. T effector cells can be converted to various types of induced Treg cells (iTregs) through engineered FOXP3 expression , or alternative strategies, including CD28 deprivation. The primary advantage of this approach is the generation of significantly more Tregs than direct isolation, thereby reducing expansion times and increasing Treg availability for therapy. However, FOXP3 expression alone does not generate the full Treg phenotype, and exposure to other molecules (e.g., TGF-β, retinoic acid, or lactoferrin) may be an essential aid or alternative path for generating iTregs. , The therapeutic potential of CAR Tregs can also be enhanced via modifications that improve their activity and localization. These modifications are essential since Tregs depend on IL-2 produced by other cells for survival and function. As IL-2 levels are often low in inflamed tissues and the CNS, co-administering IL-2 or modifying CAR Tregs to allow access to IL-2 may be critical for developing effective therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. One approach to maintain Treg exposure to IL-2 is tethering IL-2 to the high-affinity receptor (CD25/CD122/CD132), providing continuous autocrine IL-2 signaling regardless of surrounding conditions. Like CAR T cells, CAR Tregs may exhibit exhaustion after prolonged stimulation and expansion, characterized by lineage instability and reduced suppressive functions, due in part to continual low-level activation or tonic signaling. However, CAR Treg exhaustion can be minimized through various strategies, including using a Treg-stabilizing cocktail (vitamin C and an mTOR inhibitor) during ex vivo expansion and potentially by using certain costimulatory domains such as CD28 and/or 4-1BB in CAR design. CAR Tregs’ suppressive ability and resistance to exhaustion could also be improved through genetic modifications that increase the release of anti-inflammatory cytokines, neurotrophic molecules, and growth factors, an approach already used to generate pro-inflammatory cytokines in conventional CAR T cell therapies. For CAR Tregs, increased expression of CTLA-4, an immune checkpoint inhibitor that reduces APC potency and T cell proliferation, could be incorporated into the design. Treg immunosuppressive capabilities were increased by deleting PD-1, a gene associated with Treg exhaustion, and by substituting IL-10 expression under the PD-1 promoter. Another strategy to enhance therapeutic efficacy is to engineer bispecific CARs that recognize multiple antigens, thereby increasing CAR avidity. , Accurately delivering CAR Tregs to the site of inflammation is a key challenge. Tregs and other T cells can cross the BBB, primarily through a multistep process of activation, adhesion, and migration at the endothelial cell surface. The process is driven by inflammation. Cytokines and their receptors may facilitate passage. Notably, CAR Tregs express specific chemokine receptors that regulate their entry into target tissue sites. This passage can be accelerated through genetic engineering or by co-culturing CAR Tregs with vitamin D or rapamycin to promote receptor expression. , Alternatively, extracellular modifications, such as fucosylation, can enhance CAR Treg localization to inflamed tissues. Notably, CAR Tregs express specific chemokine receptors that regulate their entry into target tissue sites. This passage can be accelerated through genetic engineering or by co-culturing CAR Tregs with vitamin D or rapamycin to promote receptor expression. , Alternatively, extracellular modifications, such as fucosylation, can enhance CAR Treg localization to inflamed tissues. Fucosylation displays sialyl Lewis-X (sLe X ) on the surface of CAR T cells, facilitating interaction with E-selectin on the blood vessel endothelium and increasing tissue entry by 10-fold. Another promising method is using transient techniques such as focused ultrasound or blast shockwaves to temporarily open the BBB, aiding proper CAR Treg localization in neurodegenerative disease contexts. , Engineering CAR Tregs for neurodegenerative diseases can also incorporate safeguards to ensure these therapies can be halted if adverse effects occur. One potential safeguard is inserting a “suicide gene” that can be activated by administering a specific molecule. , , Suicide genes have been included in CAR T cell clinical trials but have not yet been adopted for CAR Tregs ( NCT02761915 , NCT03373071 , and NCT03373097 ). Another option is to induce CAR expression by transient mRNA delivery through electroporation rather than CRISPR genome editing. This approach ensures that CAR expression is temporary, since CARs are recycled and degraded. Thus, their effects will be limited in duration. , These and other major challenges must be surmounted to achieve efficacious CAR Treg therapies in the context of neurodegenerative diseases ( ). Chimeric antigen receptor Tregs for neurodegenerative diseases Alzheimer’s disease AD is the most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by memory loss, impaired executive functions, agitation, hallucinations, anxiety, depression, and aggression. Neuroinflammation plays a key role in AD, making CAR Tregs a promising treatment option. In AD, neuroinflammation is linked to the accumulation of misfolded proteins—including amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles—and resulting neuronal loss. , Whether these protein pathologies are a cause or consequence, brains affected by AD show signs of inflammation, including oxidative stress and microglial activation, , leading to increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and neurotoxic factors. , Inflammatory immune cells, including T effector cells, infiltrate the CNS from the peripheral circulation as cytokines upregulate matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which damage the BBB and fuel neuroinflammation and disease progression. , In preclinical models, blocking inflammatory pathways reduces AD pathology. Studies also show that amyloid-β-specific CD4 + T effector cells can accelerate disease progression. Additionally, Tregs isolated from patients with AD tend to be fewer and less effective at immunosuppression. , There is evidence of an imbalance between circulating Th17 cells and Tregs in patients with AD. Genetic risk factors for AD are often related to immune function, further strengthening the connection between neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. Despite conflicting data, several studies support the potential of CAR-Treg therapies in AD by demonstrating Treg’s neuroprotective effects. In AD mouse models, adoptive transfer of amyloid-β-specific Tregs demonstrates the inhibition of microglial activation and improved cognition, along with reductions in amyloid load, tau hyperphosphorylation, and a spectrum of neuroinflammatory biomarkers. , , Our own laboratory’s proof-of-concept study, in which Tregs were genetically engineered to express TCRs specific for amyloid-β, resulted in reduced immune suppression and decreased microglial activation and amyloid loads in an AD mouse model. These investigations were among the first to generate Treg antigen specificity for neuroprotection in AD models. Recently, amyloid-specific Treg therapy for AD was tested in a small trial ( NCT05016427 ). CD4 + CD25hiCD127lo Tregs were isolated from the blood of six patients with AD and expanded with IL-2 and amyloid-β. Due to the small sample size, no definitive conclusions on human efficacy could be drawn. These observations, taken together, support the idea that delivering amyloid-specific human Tregs for AD may provide therapeutic benefits. The combined efforts suggest the potential to develop effective CAR Treg therapies for AD. A major challenge is that amyloid proteins are widely distributed throughout the body. Since most amyloids do not cause disease, , targeting all amyloids could lead to unwanted side effects and diminish therapy effectiveness by diverting CAR Tregs from pathogenic forms. To address this, our laboratories are developing antibodies specific to the soluble oligomers, protofibrils, and insoluble fibrillary forms. CARs now in development have also been shown to distinguish between tau tangles and different amyloid peptides. This has enabled the engineering of Tregs with highly specific tau- or amyloid-specific CARs. Using scFvs based on FDA-approved antibodies can facilitate clinical translation. In addition to these efforts, CAR Tregs have responded to amyloid-β and suppressed inflammation in vitro . Parkinson’s disease PD, the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after AD, also demonstrates neuroinflammatory pathology. The symptoms of PD include motor impairments such as tremor, slowed movement, and poor balance. Non-motor symptoms include sleep disorders, anosmia, constipation, and depression. Shaking, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability are the most common symptoms. , Each motor impairment results mainly from the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, a process associated with α-syn aggregates, or Lewy bodies (LBs). , Neurodegeneration occurs alongside microglial activation and the subsequent recruitment of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells into affected brain regions. PD shows increased levels of inflammatory biomarkers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukins (IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-8), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interferon gamma (IFN-γ), and reactive oxygen species. These markers are found in the brain, peripheral lymphoid organs, and blood, and their levels are linked to a higher risk of dementia and cognitive decline. Some T cells from patients with PD are immunoreactive for α-syn, supporting the idea that this induces pro-inflammatory interactions. , As in AD, genetic risk factors for PD are often connected to immune system dysfunction. , Evidence indicates that patients with PD have fewer resting Tregs and more activated Tregs, with higher Treg levels associated with less severe cognitive impairment. While the data suggest potential benefits of CAR Tregs in PD, further early research is needed. Inducing Tregs using GM-CSF or anti-CD28 antibodies has shown neuroprotective effects in MPTP mouse models of PD, , and early clinical trials have safely administered granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF, sargramostim) to patients with PD ( NCT03790670 , NCT01882010 ). These data demonstrated Treg induction and a potential for neurorestoration. The datasets are supported by adoptive transfer of Tregs, which has also shown a neuroprotective promise in preclinical PD studies. Recent research from our lab has buoyed this concept by demonstrating that antigen-specific Tregs have therapeutic advantages over natural and nonspecific Treg infusions. However, clinical translation needs to overcome MHC restrictions. , CAR Tregs may also play a supporting role in other PD treatments. One study showed that co-transplanting dopamine neurons with Tregs reduced inflammation and tissue rejection and improved graft tolerance in PD mice. Using CAR Tregs instead of polyclonal Tregs could improve these outcomes. Multiple sclerosis MS is a relapsing-remitting CNS autoimmune disease in which a patient’s innate and adaptive immune cells—microglia, NK cells, B cells, and T cells—attack the myelin sheath surrounding spinal nerves, causing periodic episodes of severe pain and progressive neurodegeneration. , These episodes result from interactions between activated microglia and T cells and are associated with Treg dysfunction, , although no clear disease-causing antigens such as amyloid-β or α-syn have been identified. While conventional CAR T cell therapies have been used to eliminate autoreactive B cells and effectively “reset” the immune system in MS, , , Treg therapies are also emerging as a potential treatment option. Tregs can promote remyelination in mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Several research groups have induced the formation of myelin-specific Tregs in vivo without CAR engineering, showing how these antigen-specific Tregs protect myelin sheaths and reverse disease progression in EAE mice. , TCR-engineered Tregs targeting myelin basic protein (MBP) also suppress MOG-induced EAE, demonstrating the ability of CAR Tregs to combat autoimmunity through bystander effects that transcend antigen specificity. Building on these findings, one group developed and tested myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG)-specific CAR Tregs. They chose CD4 + CD45RA+CD127loCD25hi Tregs as the therapeutic vehicle due to their epigenetic stability and resistance to Th17 conversion. CAR expression was induced using a lentivirus, and the resulting receptors were engineered to include a CD28 − CD3ζ intracellular domain. When administered to EAE mice, MOG CAR Tregs localized to the CNS, delayed the onset of EAE, and reduced the activity of pro-inflammatory pathogenic immune cells. Importantly, these MOG CAR Tregs were developed using methods currently being used in a kidney transplant clinical trial ( NCT04817774 ), facilitating clinical translation. Another group selected CD4 + CD25hiCD127lo Tregs from healthy human blood and engineered CAR Tregs targeting MOG and myelin basic protein (MBP), demonstrating therapeutic efficacy in EAE mice. When administered to EAE mice, MOG CAR Tregs localized to the CNS, delayed the onset of EAE, and reduced the activity of pro-inflammatory pathogenic immune cells. Importantly, these MOG CAR Tregs were developed using methods currently being used in a kidney transplant clinical trial ( NCT04817774 ), facilitating clinical translation. Another group selected CD4 + CD25hiCD127lo Tregs from healthy human blood and engineered CAR Tregs targeting MOG and myelin basic protein (MBP), demonstrating therapeutic efficacy in EAE mice. In a different approach, one team used a retroviral vector to engineer CAR Tregs that target a receptor (XCR1) on the surface of dendritic cells (DCs), and a separate CAR Treg targeting MOG for comparison. They slightly delayed EAE onset in mice by leveraging their CAR Tregs' ability to suppress the DC-mediated activation of T effector cells via antigen presentation. However, MOG CAR Tregs suppressed EAE more effectively. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ALS is an autoimmune disease characterized by the progressive loss of CNS motor neurons, leading to fatal paralysis. Similar to other neurodegenerative conditions, ALS progression has been linked to microglia-mediated neuroinflammation. Genetic risk factors for ALS include mutations in the SOD1 gene, which encodes superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1), an enzyme that protects against oxidative damage and neutralizes toxic byproducts of inflammation. , The potential role of Tregs in treating ALS is supported by observational studies showing that patients with higher Treg levels tend to experience slower disease progression than patients with lower Treg levels. Additionally, patients with ALS exhibit reduced expression of full-length Foxp3, leading to functional deficits affecting Tregs. Treg therapies have shown early promise in preclinical studies and clinical trials for ALS. Adoptive transfer of polyclonal Tregs extends the lifespan of an ALS mouse model. In a clinical trial, patients with ALS were treated with autologous polyclonal Tregs and IL-2 for a year ( NCT04055623 ). The results demonstrated that Treg therapy was well-tolerated and increased Treg suppressive function. However, conclusions about the treatment’s efficacy in slowing ALS progression could not be drawn due to the study’s small size. The first steps toward developing CAR Treg therapies for ALS were taken by Graber et al., who developed CAR Tregs targeting aberrant SOD1. These CAR Tregs expressed a CD28 − CD3ζ intracellular domain and selectively bound mutant SOD1 over the wild-type enzyme, suppressing inflammatory responses against mutated SOD1 in vitro . In a follow-up study, the same team engineered SOD1-specific CAR Tregs that co-express BDNF. In an ALS mouse model, these cells delayed disease onset, reduced CNS inflammation, and lengthened lifespans. Conclusions and future directions Neurodegenerative diseases are a relatively new application of CAR T cell therapy ( ). However, their path to clinical use has been paved by extensive research that prepared both conventional CAR T cell therapies and CAR Treg therapies for patient use in other conditions (GvHD, type 1 diabetes). This provides developers of CAR Treg therapies for neurodegenerative diseases with a solid foundation, including multiple generations of CAR designs, good manufacturing practice (GMP) protocols for isolating clinical-grade Tregs, and modifications to enhance CAR Treg functions, as well as common pitfalls to avoid. The remaining challenges to clinical translation mainly involve issues unique to neurodegenerative diseases ( ). Perhaps the biggest hurdle is identifying suitable antigen targets that minimize off-target effects while offering clear benefits in slowing or reversing the disease. The more specific the target, the higher the chances of success. Considering the limited benefits shown by polyclonal Tregs and other nonspecific Treg therapies in some trials, CAR Tregs targeting common CNS antigens and suppressing inflammation through bystander effects seem less ideal, although they may be necessary in cases such as MS. Another challenge is engineering cells that can specifically cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Potential solutions include mechanical methods such as opening the BBB by focused ultrasound or chemical modifications, such as chemokine receptors or fucosylation. These approaches could facilitate CAR Treg entry into the targeted area. In any case, because the BBB is more permeable during inflammation, this naturally facilitates CAR Treg localization to the site. Efforts to adapt traditional CAR T cell therapies for glioblastoma may serve as a useful reference.
